newsitem.title: USA: Jury seated for federal trial of Ariz. governor.
newsitem.headline: Jury seated for federal trial of Ariz. governor.

text.p: A 12-member jury was sworn in Thursday to hear Arizona Gov. Fife Symington's federal trial on fraud, extortion and perjury charges.
The jury, with five alternates, was selected after three days of questioning in U.S. District Court. Once seated, the nine men and eight women listened as the indictment against Symington was read.
Afterward, Symington leaned over to family members and said in an audible whisper: "Tomorrow is what we call our return of serve" -- a reference to Friday's opening arguments.
"Sorry you had to sit through all that nonsense. We're on our way now," the governor said.

Symington, a 51-year-old colorful Republican, faces 22 felony charges. Federal prosecutors will try to prove to the jury that Symington committed fraud, extortion and perjury in connection with real estate deals during the last decade.
If convicted on even a single count, the two-term governor would be booted from the office he has held since 1991. He also faces a possible prison term.

During the trial, which was expected to last 12 weeks, prosecutors will detail what they claim were lies told by Symington from the mid-1980s to early 1990s when he was a developer, to secure credit and business and personal loans.

The government contends Symington made false statements to lenders to prevent his real estate empire from crumbling. Prosecutors also will try to prove Symington extorted an agreement from six union pension funds to release him from a personal loan guarantee he made to obtain a $10 million loan for a shopping center in downtown Phoenix.
The government also will try to prove the governor lied under oath during court proceedings when he filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in September, 1995.
The defense will argue that Symington made only inadvertent errors of omission and that they did not affect his getting loans.
The charges stem from a probe into the 1989 collapse of Southwest Savings & Loan Association. Symington served on the thrift's board of directors.
After settling the case, the U.S. Attorney's office in Los Angeles continued its probe into the governor's financial dealings for several years. Last June, Symington was indicted.
